title: Shoftim: judges at the gates (Deuteronomy 16:18)
hook: judges in every town; Hasidic teachers read the gates as eyes, ears and mouth

segments.voice: Yesterday, the pilgrims who gave according to the gift of their hand. Your line was according to your blessing. What did you give from your surplus? Today a new portion, Shoftim, starts at the town gate. Day five hundred two.

Where would you go to settle a family dispute in the world of the Bible? Not a building with columns. The gate. In the Bible, a town gate is more than a door in the wall. Elders sit there. Deals are witnessed there. In the book of Ruth, Boaz goes up to the gate, sits down, and settles a family matter in front of ten elders. Everything that comes into the town, people, goods, news, trouble, comes through the gate, and whoever sits there decides what to do about it. That's where the new portion begins.
screen: `TO SETTLE IT, GO TO THE GATE.` →`BOAZ SITS AT THE GATE.` → `EVERYTHING COMES THROUGH.`

segments.voice: The first verse, in the old Jewish translation: "Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates." Shoftim means judges, and it names the portion. The plain sense is civic. Every town needs courts, and people to enforce what courts decide, right where life passes through. Justice shouldn't be a long trip to a distant capital. It should sit at your own gate. But notice the odd little word thee. Shalt thou make thee. In Hebrew, lecha: for yourself. Judges for yourself? Later teachers seized on that. Hasidic masters, building on earlier mystics, read the verse inward. A person is a town too, they said, with gates of their own. The eyes, the ears, the mouth, and some add the nostrils. Everything that enters you comes through those gates: what you look at, what you listen to, what you take in. And everything that leaves you goes out through one of them: what you say. So set judges at your gates. Not to shut them. A town with its gates welded shut starves. But to notice what's coming in and going out, and to decide. And there's a calendar reason this reading lands well. Shoftim is usually read around the start of Elul, the month before Rosh Hashanah, a season set aside for taking stock. A portion about courts at the gates arrives just as people start judging their own year.
screen: `SHOFTIM: JUDGES.` · `JUSTICE AT YOUR OWN GATE.` · `LECHA: FOR YOURSELF.` · `EYES, EARS, MOUTH.` · then, large: `GUARD YOUR GATES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: guard one of your own gates. Settle, and breathe. Close your eyes, and notice them resting. Notice your ears, what's coming in right now. Notice your mouth, closed. Now think about the last day. What came in through your eyes that you'd rather not have let in? What through your ears? What went out of your mouth that you'd take back? Pick one gate. Not all of them. Decide one small thing that gate's judge will watch for today. The bell holds the time.
Shoftim. Judges. The name of the portion, from its first command: judges and officers in all your gates.
Your line: guard your gates. Today, stand at the gate you chose, and let one thing not come in, or not go out. Day five hundred two.

howItsDone: Shoftim is usually read in synagogues around the start of Elul, the month before Rosh Hashanah, and Hasidic and other teachers often use its opening verse to speak about guarding the eyes, ears and mouth as part of the season's self-examination.

what a scholar hears: the singular lecha, for yourself, invites the Hasidic reading of the body's gates; Ruth 4 shows a court sitting at the gate.

notes: Deuteronomy 16:18 quoted from JPS 1917 from memory; verify.

The reading of 'gates' as the body's openings (seven gates: two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, mouth) is found in the Shelah and many Hasidic works (e.g., Siftei Tzaddik, Kedushat Levi traditions); a Keeper should supply a specific citation.
Ruth 4:1–2: Boaz at the gate with ten elders.

Shoftim is generally read in Elul; confirm for leap/non-leap years. Reviewer softened howItsDone to 'usually ... around the start of Elul', since in some years it falls at the end of Av or on Rosh Chodesh Elul.
